title: White House Clears Labor Department Plan to Overhaul PERM Green Card Rules
excerpt: The proposed PERM modernization (RIN 1205-AC29) cleared OIRA review on October 23 and heads to the Federal Register, with recruitment standards, layoff rules and nondiscrimination requirements in scope.
body:
• The White House's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs completed its review of the Department of Labor's proposed PERM overhaul on October 23 — the last step before the proposal is published in the Federal Register.
  • The proposal (RIN 1205-AC29) is expected to address minimum recruitment standards, rules on US-worker layoffs, and employer nondiscrimination requirements for green card sponsorship.
  • Nothing changes for current applicants yet: a public comment period of 30 to 60 days follows publication, and the rules take effect only after a final rule is issued.
  • PERM is the mandatory first step for most employment-based green cards, including the EB-2 and EB-3 categories where Indian applicants form the largest group — if your employer is preparing a PERM filing, it still proceeds under the existing rules today.

A Department of Labor proposal to modernize PERM, the permanent labor certification process at the heart of employment-based green cards, has cleared White House review, Bloomberg Law reported. The plan, tracked as RIN 1205-AC29, completed review at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on October 23, a step that signals public release of the proposal could come soon.

The regulations governing PERM have not been substantially updated in roughly two decades. The program is the Labor Department's test that no qualified US worker is available for a job before an employer can sponsor a foreign worker for permanent residence, and it is the first step in most employment-based green card cases.

What the overhaul is expected to cover

The full text of the proposal has not been published yet. Based on the administration's regulatory agenda and reporting by SHRM, the proposal is expected to address minimum recruitment standards — how employers must advertise and test the labor market — rules related to US-worker layoffs, and employer nondiscrimination requirements. Reporting on the cleared review also points to recruitment modernization and record-retention provisions among the core areas in scope.

That combination matters for Indian professionals in the EB-2 and EB-3 queues, who account for the largest share of PERM filings. Recruitment standards determine how a job must be advertised before a filing; layoff rules can pause or complicate sponsorship at employers that have recently cut US staff in the same occupation and area; and nondiscrimination provisions govern how employers document why US applicants were or were not qualified.

An enforcement crackdown is running in parallel

The proposal advances amid a broader Trump administration enforcement push against the PERM program itself. At a White House event on October 8, Vice President JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspension of eight employers from PERM — Microsoft and Adobe, and six IT services firms: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini.

"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies."

— Keith Sonderling, US Secretary of Labor

Officials linked the suspensions to alleged fraud and to employers using skilled-worker programs while laying off US employees. Microsoft responded that about 80 percent of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year concerned extensions or changes of status for existing employees rather than new hires, and that it pays H-1B employees the same as comparable colleagues. The government has announced suspensions and investigations; it has not published an adjudicated finding of fraud against the named companies.

What happens next

Publication in the Federal Register is the next step. A proposed rule is then open for public comment — typically 30 or 60 days — after which the Labor Department must review comments before issuing a final rule with an effective date. Until that final rule exists, PERM filings continue under the current regulations, unchanged since their last comprehensive update in 2005.

For workers mid-process, the practical position is unchanged today: a pending PERM is judged under today's rules, and employers at the eight suspended firms remain frozen regardless of the rulemaking. The proposal's text, once published, will show whether the overhaul tightens recruitment in ways that lengthen PERM timelines — the detail that will decide how much this matters to the Indian green card queue.
